paragraphs: Estimating counterfactuals over time means asking how outcomes might have changed under different treatment histories. ACTIN addresses this problem with two cooperating modules: one learns representations that reduce confounding bias, and the other combines information across time. This division connects two challenges that matter for treatment planning: making treatment comparisons more balanced and accounting for how earlier treatments affect later outcomes.

The balancing module uses an adversarial method based on distributions. Its purpose is to learn balanced representations across different treatment types, extending beyond the classification-based approaches discussed in the paper. The integrating module then applies Temporal Integration Predicting, which considers treatments and balanced representations from the start of the sequence through the current time.

That broader history distinguishes the method from Direct Predicting, which uses only current treatments and representations. It allows ACTIN to capture long-range dependencies and interactions between treatments over time. Across synthetic and real-world datasets, the authors report state-of-the-art performance and efficiency even with simple underlying models, supporting the usefulness of the framework beyond a particular base architecture.
icml-2024-a-dual-module-framework-for-co.tldr: ACTIN combines distribution-based balancing with treatment-history integration to improve counterfactual estimation over time.

paragraphs: Fitted Q-evaluation estimates how well a target policy would perform using previously collected data from another policy. This paper studies how accurately it can do so when its value-function model is either parametric or nonparametric. The central questions concern how estimation error changes with the amount of data, the length of the decision sequence, and assumptions about probability ratios.

Under a completeness assumption on the Q-functions, the authors show that both kinds of estimator can achieve the optimal sample-size rate of 1/√n for a fixed horizon. They describe this assumption as mild in the nonparametric setting. The result establishes that moving beyond parametric models need not sacrifice the optimal rate for estimating a policy's value.

The analysis also separates sample-size effects from horizon effects. With an additional realizability assumption on the probability-ratio functions, the error rate improves from T^1.5/√n to T/√n. This matches the sharpest known tabular bound cited by the authors. The improvement is conditional on that extra assumption, clarifying which modeling properties support better accuracy over longer decision sequences.
icml-2024-a-fine-grained-analysis-of-fit.tldr: The paper establishes optimal sample-size rates for parametric and nonparametric fitted Q-evaluation and identifies an assumption that improves horizon dependence.

paragraphs: Maximal coding rate reduction, or MCR², is an objective for learning compact representations that retain useful structure. Its global optima had already been studied, but those best possible solutions did not explain the rest of the optimization landscape. This paper addresses that gap by characterizing local optima, global optima, and the other critical points of the objective.

The authors show that every local or global maximizer corresponds to a representation that is low-dimensional, discriminative, and diverse. This matters because desirable representations are therefore associated with local maximizers as well as globally best solutions. They also prove that every critical point is either a local maximizer or a strict saddle point, giving a precise description of the remaining stationary configurations.

Together, these findings provide theoretical support for using MCR² with first-order optimization methods. The contribution concerns the geometry of the objective and the quality of its maximizers, rather than only examples of successful training. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets illustrate the established properties and complement the theoretical characterization.
icml-2024-a-global-geometric-analysis-of.tldr: Every MCR² maximizer yields a compact, discriminative, diverse representation, and every other critical point is a strict saddle.

paragraphs: For linearly separable classification data, this paper examines the tendency of gradient-based algorithms to maximize the separating margin. Its focus is the speed of that process. The authors analyze the velocity field associated with gradients and normalized gradients to understand how their update directions influence progress toward a maximum-margin solution.

That analysis motivates Progressive Rescaling Gradient Descent, or PRGD. The authors prove that PRGD maximizes the margin at an exponential rate, compared with the polynomial rates of the existing algorithms considered in the work. They also identify mild conditions on the data distribution under which ordinary and normalized gradient descent provably fail to maximize the margin efficiently.

Synthetic and real-world experiments support the theoretical findings. The paper additionally reports promising generalization behavior when PRGD is used on linearly nonseparable datasets and deep neural networks. Those broader observations are empirical extensions of the method's appeal; the stated exponential margin-maximization result belongs to the linearly separable setting studied in the theory.
icml-2024-achieving-margin-maximization-.tldr: PRGD uses progressive rescaling to achieve provably exponential margin maximization for linearly separable classification.

paragraphs: Quantile regression offers an alternative to least-squares regression that is useful for robustness to outliers and heterogeneous data. This paper studies its distributed, high-dimensional form, including both coefficient estimation and support recovery: identifying which variables have nonzero coefficients. The main obstacle is that the usual quantile-regression loss is nonsmooth, complicating distributed computation and its theoretical analysis.

The authors transform the original problem into a least-squares optimization and introduce a double-smoothing approach. This extends an earlier Newton-type distributed method while removing its restrictive assumption that the error term and covariates are independent. The resulting algorithm is designed to use both computation and communication efficiently.

The theoretical results establish a near-oracle convergence rate and high support-recovery accuracy after a constant number of iterations. These findings address both the accuracy of estimated effects and the identification of relevant variables. Experiments on synthetic examples and a real-data application further support the method's effectiveness, connecting the distributed optimization design to its statistical objectives.
icml-2024-distributed-high-dimensional-q.tldr: A double-smoothing method makes distributed high-dimensional quantile regression efficient while providing strong estimation and variable-selection guarantees.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction returns a set of plausible labels with a prescribed coverage rate. Its practical use usually depends on observing true labels for model training and calibration. This paper addresses online settings with bandit feedback, where the learner only discovers whether its chosen label was correct. An incorrect choice rules out that label without revealing the correct one.

This feedback creates two connected difficulties: incomplete information for learning and sparse labeled data for estimating calibration quantiles. Bandit Class-specific Conformal Prediction, or BCCP, tackles both through an unbiased estimate of a quantity involving the true label. It uses that estimate within stochastic gradient descent to train the model and produce prediction sets.

BCCP provides coverage guarantees at the level of individual classes, making the reliability target more specific than a single overall coverage figure. The contribution extends set-valued prediction to an online environment where complete labels are unavailable at each step. Its significance lies in connecting limited correctness feedback to learning and calibration within one approach.
icml-2024-efficient-online-set-valued-cl.tldr: BCCP enables online prediction sets with class-specific coverage guarantees when feedback reveals only whether the chosen label was correct.

paragraphs: EfficientZero V2 targets a practical reinforcement-learning problem: learning useful behavior from limited interaction data across different kinds of tasks. The paper builds on EfficientZero and broadens its reach to settings with discrete or continuous actions. It also covers both visual observations and low-dimensional inputs, making breadth across environments a central part of the contribution.

These combinations matter because a generally useful learning framework must handle variation in both what an agent observes and how it acts. The authors introduce a series of improvements intended to make that broader coverage sample-efficient. Their evaluation asks whether the resulting framework performs strongly when the amount of available training data is restricted.

The reported results show significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in the evaluated limited-data tasks. Against DreamerV3, EfficientZero V2 achieves better outcomes in 50 of 66 tasks across benchmarks including Atari 100k, Proprio Control, and Vision Control. This supports its empirical breadth while preserving the distinction between strong performance across many tasks and superiority on every evaluated task.
icml-2024-efficientzero-v2-mastering-dis.tldr: EfficientZero V2 extends sample-efficient reinforcement learning across action and observation types, outperforming DreamerV3 on 50 of 66 evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: EvoluNet studies knowledge transfer between graph domains that change over time and have different data distributions. Its setting provides label-rich source graphs and label-scarce target graphs for the previous T timestamps. The goal is to improve prediction in the target domain at timestamp T+1, accounting for both evolving graphs and changing differences between domains.

The authors derive a generalization bound that highlights domain evolution and source–target discrepancy as major influences on target performance. This motivates two parts of the framework. A transformer-based temporal encoder represents how the domains evolve, while a dynamic domain-unification module learns representations that are invariant across the source and target domains.

The approach therefore treats temporal change and transfer mismatch as connected problems. Its reported improvements over state-of-the-art models reach up to 12.1%, supporting the effectiveness of transferring knowledge between dynamic graphs in the evaluated settings. The theoretical contribution explains why both kinds of change deserve attention, while the framework turns that guidance into a concrete representation-learning strategy.
icml-2024-evolunet-advancing-dynamic-non.tldr: EvoluNet combines temporal modeling and domain-invariant representations to transfer knowledge between changing source and target graphs.

paragraphs: Stochastic weight averaging has demonstrated empirical advantages over stochastic gradient descent, but its theoretical explanation has been more limited. This paper studies generalization in nonconvex settings with sampling either with or without replacement. These settings broaden the analysis beyond the convex, replacement-sampling conditions that had received much of the theoretical attention.

The difficulty comes from the history carried by averaging. A stability analysis must account for historical gradients, whose bounds depend on earlier steps and become nested. The authors use mathematical induction to obtain a recursive representation that bounds the gradient at each step, making this accumulated dependence manageable.

Using that representation, the paper establishes stability bounds for both sampling schemes and derives sharper generalization bounds for stochastic weight averaging than for stochastic gradient descent. The finding supplies theoretical support for the benefits of averaging under the analyzed nonconvex conditions. Experiments on several benchmarks support the theoretical results, linking the mathematical treatment of training history to observed generalization behavior.
icml-2024-generalization-analysis-of-sto.tldr: The paper derives sharper generalization bounds for stochastic weight averaging than SGD in nonconvex settings under both major sampling schemes.

paragraphs: LatentTracer asks whether an image can be attributed to a particular latent generative model without adding a watermark or modifying training or generation. This addresses a constraint of tracing methods that require extra operations before an image is examined. The goal is model-specific attribution: distinguishing images from the inspected model from other images.

The method searches for a latent input that allows the inspected model to reconstruct the image well. It uses gradient-based latent inversion, with an encoder supplying the starting point. The authors identify this encoder-based initialization as critical to the approach's success, connecting effective attribution to how the reconstruction search begins.

Experiments with latent generative models, including Stable Diffusion, show high attribution accuracy and efficiency. The findings suggest that the decoder may leave a naturally occurring signature in generated images, even without an artificial watermark. The paper presents this as an intriguing possibility supported by the results, rather than a universal guarantee that every generated image can be traced.
icml-2024-how-to-trace-latent-generative.tldr: LatentTracer uses encoder-initialized latent inversion to attribute images to a specific generator without adding artificial watermarks.

paragraphs: InstructRetro investigates whether retrieval-augmented pretraining can strengthen a language model before instruction tuning. The authors build Retro 48B by continuing the pretraining of a 43B GPT model on 100 billion additional tokens, using retrieval from 1.2 trillion tokens. This expands the scale of the retrieval-pretrained models discussed in the paper.

Retro 48B substantially improves perplexity over the GPT 43B counterpart trained on 1.2 trillion tokens, with 2.58% additional GPU hours. After instruction tuning, InstructRetro also improves zero-shot task performance. The reported average gains over the instruction-tuned GPT counterpart are 7% across eight short-form question-answering and reading-comprehension tasks, 10% across four long-form question-answering tasks, and 16% across three summarization tasks.

A notable finding is that removing InstructRetro's encoder and using its decoder backbone yields comparable results. This suggests that retrieval during continued pretraining can improve the decoder in a way that remains useful after the encoder is removed. The paper therefore supports retrieval-augmented pretraining as a promising route to stronger instruction-tuned decoders.
icml-2024-instructretro-instruction-tuni.tldr: InstructRetro improves zero-shot performance through retrieval-augmented pretraining before instruction tuning, with comparable results after removing its encoder.

paragraphs: PHAZE jointly searches for accelerator hardware and the strategy for distributing deep-learning training across devices. These choices interact because computational capacity, memory, and data distribution all affect execution. The paper treats hardware architecture and placement as a combined optimization problem, allowing decisions on one side to inform the other.

The hardware search varies the number and dimensions of tensor and vector units, along with on-chip and off-chip memory. It also chooses microbatch size and whether activations should be stored or recomputed. For each candidate architecture, an integer linear program finds an optimal operator-execution schedule on the accelerator.

Those scheduling results feed a dynamic-programming method that selects device placement using combinations of data, pipeline, and tensor model parallelism. This connects individual-accelerator execution to the organization of training across multiple accelerators. The authors report higher throughput on large language models than TPUv4 and the Spotlight accelerator-search framework, supporting the value of coordinating architecture design with distributed execution choices.
icml-2024-integrated-hardware-architectu.tldr: PHAZE co-optimizes accelerator architecture, execution scheduling, and device placement to improve distributed language-model training throughput.

paragraphs: LESR addresses the information an agent receives as its state representation. Conventional representations can leave out details that matter for a task, making it harder for a value network to connect states with rewards. Learning those connections from extensive interaction can require many samples and substantial training time.

The method uses a large language model to generate task-related state-representation code autonomously. This puts the language model's knowledge into the representation used by reinforcement learning, with minimal human intervention. The generated representations are intended to improve the continuity of the network's mappings and make training more efficient.

Experiments report high sample efficiency and improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, averaging 29% in accumulated reward on MuJoCo tasks and 30% in success rates on Gym-Robotics tasks. These are separate improvements in different measures, each tied to its evaluated task family. The results support using language-model-generated representation code as a practical way to supply task information that the learner would otherwise need to extract through experience.
icml-2024-llm-empowered-state-representa.tldr: LESR uses language models to generate task-specific state-representation code that improves reinforcement-learning sample efficiency and performance.

paragraphs: MC-GTA groups temporal or spatial observations while accounting for a supplied distance metric. Its starting point is that feature similarity and metric distance can be related, a relationship called metric autocorrelation. Existing metric-constrained clustering methods overlook this information, while strong model-based approaches also face computational instability and complexity.

The proposed objective consists of weighted pairwise terms combining feature similarity with metric autocorrelation. Feature similarity uses squared Wasserstein-2 distance, and autocorrelation uses a new multivariate extension of the classic semivariogram. The authors show that this objective effectively minimizes hinge-loss penalties for within-cluster pairs that fail goodness-of-fit tests for sharing a distribution.

This gives the grouping objective a statistical interpretation while incorporating how similarity varies with distance. Experiments on one- and two-dimensional synthetic and real datasets show improvements over strong baselines of up to 14.3% in ARI and 32.1% in NMI, alongside more than tenfold speedup and stabler optimization. These reported gains support both the clustering value of autocorrelation and the computational benefits of the formulation.
icml-2024-mc-gta-metric-constrained-mode.tldr: MC-GTA combines feature similarity and metric autocorrelation in a statistically motivated clustering objective with reported accuracy and speed gains.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning models the distribution of returns. This paper proves that doing so can yield second-order guarantees in both online and offline reinforcement learning with function approximation. These guarantees depend on return variance, making them sensitive to the particular problem instance. The authors show they are tighter than previously known small-loss bounds for distributional reinforcement learning.

The results include second-order bounds for low-rank decision processes and offline reinforcement learning, which the authors identify as the first such results to their knowledge. For contextual bandits, the one-step setting, a distributional optimism algorithm simultaneously achieves a second-order worst-case regret bound and a second-order bound that depends on reward gaps.

The analysis follows optimism in the face of uncertainty and avoids weighted regression. Real-world contextual-bandit experiments also demonstrate benefits from distributional learning. Together, the theory and experiments strengthen the case that learning return distributions can improve guarantees as well as empirical behavior, with the theoretical advantage explicitly reflecting variation in returns.
icml-2024-more-benefits-of-being-distrib.tldr: Distributional reinforcement learning can achieve tighter, variance-sensitive guarantees across online RL, offline RL, and contextual bandits.

paragraphs: This paper treats prompt engineering for text-to-image diffusion models as an optimization problem over discrete language choices. It introduces a gradient-based framework for searching that space. Two obstacles shape the design: the enormous number of possible words and prompts, and the difficulty of obtaining gradients through diffusion inference and a nondifferentiable embedding lookup.

To reduce the search space, the method dynamically constructs compact sets of words relevant to the user's input. It also introduces Shortcut Text Gradient, a substitute for the difficult text gradient that can be computed with constant memory and runtime. Together, these components make the discrete search more manageable without requiring optimization over the entire language space at once.

Evaluations use prompts drawn from DiffusionDB, ChatGPT, and COCO. The results suggest that the method can find prompts that substantially improve image faithfulness, as well as adversarial prompts that severely undermine it. The contribution therefore connects prompt enhancement and prompt-based attacks through a common optimization framework, exposing both useful control and vulnerability in text-conditioned generation.
icml-2024-on-discrete-prompt-optimizatio.tldr: A compact word search and shortcut gradient enable discrete prompt optimization that can improve or undermine diffusion-image faithfulness.

paragraphs: Pi-DUAL tackles learning from incorrect labels using privileged information: information available during training but unavailable at test time. Earlier methods using this extra information had not consistently prevented overfitting to label noise better than methods without it. The paper introduces an architecture designed to distinguish the learning of valid labels from the fitting of wrong ones.

Pi-DUAL splits its output logits into two terms. A prediction term uses conventional input features, while a noise-fitting term depends only on privileged information. A gate controlled by the privileged information adjusts the emphasis between them. This lets the model implicitly separate the learning paths associated with clean and noisy labels.

The authors report significant improvements on privileged-information benchmarks, including a 6.8% improvement on ImageNet-PI and state-of-the-art test accuracy. Pi-DUAL also outperforms strong methods at identifying noisy samples after training. These findings support using training-only information to guide where label fitting occurs, with benefits both for predictive performance and for locating potentially incorrect training labels.
icml-2024-pi-dual-using-privileged-infor.tldr: Pi-DUAL uses training-only privileged information to separate prediction from noise fitting, improving accuracy and noisy-label identification.

paragraphs: PACE addresses explanations of vision-transformer predictions after the model has been trained. The paper first specifies five desired properties: faithfulness, stability, sparsity, multi-level structure, and parsimony. It argues that existing feature-attribution and conceptual approaches do not comprehensively satisfy these requirements, establishing explicit criteria for evaluating an explanation method.

The proposed framework uses variational Bayesian modeling to represent distributions of image-patch embeddings and their relationship with the transformer's predictions. Its explanations describe concepts at the patch level. Modeling the joint distribution connects those concepts to the model's outputs, making the explanation framework about how patch representations and predictions relate.

Patch-level explanations also connect image-level and dataset-level accounts, giving PACE its multi-level structure. Qualitative analysis examines the distributions of these concepts, while experiments on synthetic and real datasets compare the method with existing approaches. The reported results show advantages across the paper's defined desiderata. This supports PACE as a structured probabilistic approach to conceptual explanation under those evaluation criteria.
icml-2024-probabilistic-conceptual-expla.tldr: PACE models patch concepts probabilistically to explain vision transformers across patch, image, and dataset levels.

paragraphs: This paper tackles interpretability in reinforcement learning, focusing on the difficulty of understanding reward functions and the policies they produce. It approaches sequential decision-making through probabilistic inference, which provides mathematical tools for reasoning about stochastic dynamics and interpreting policy optimization. The proposed method is Adaptive Wasserstein Variational Optimization, or AWaVO.

AWaVO uses formal methods to address three aspects of interpretability: convergence guarantees, training transparency, and interpretation of decisions within the method itself. This makes interpretability part of the optimization framework. The paper reports a global convergence rate of Θ(1/√T), supplying a quantitative guarantee alongside its treatment of training and decision interpretation.

The authors demonstrate the approach in simulations and real-world quadrotor tasks. Comparisons with TRPO-IPO, PCPO, and CRPO empirically support a reasonable trade-off between performance and sufficient interpretability. The stated outcome is a balance between these objectives, with formal convergence analysis and practical evaluations contributing different kinds of evidence for the proposed framework.
icml-2024-probabilistic-constrained-rein.tldr: AWaVO combines probabilistic policy optimization with formal interpretability and convergence guarantees, demonstrated in simulation and quadrotor tasks.

paragraphs: Proteus is a diffusion model for generating new protein backbones. The paper addresses a trade-off in existing approaches: strong models can depend on large pretrained structure-prediction networks, while alternatives trained from scratch have lagged in performance. Its goal is to produce highly designable structures efficiently without relying on structure-prediction pretraining.

The network combines graph-based triangle methods with a multi-track interaction architecture. These are the central architectural components presented as enabling the model to work without the pretrained structure-prediction machinery used by approaches such as RFdiffusion. The contribution links this architecture to both generation quality and efficiency in de novo backbone design.

The authors evaluate Proteus through computational assessments and experimental characterization. They report strong success and support for its ability to generate highly designable backbones efficiently. The findings suggest that dependence on structure-prediction pretraining can be removed while retaining useful protein-design capabilities. The broader impact on protein design is presented as potential, grounded in the model's demonstrated backbone-generation results.
icml-2024-proteus-exploring-protein-stru.tldr: Proteus generates highly designable protein backbones efficiently using a diffusion architecture that requires no structure-prediction pretraining.

paragraphs: RL-VLM-F addresses the effort required to design reward functions for reinforcement learning. It generates rewards using a text description of the task goal and visual observations from the agent. A vision-language foundation model provides the feedback, reducing the need for humans to repeatedly design and adjust rewards for each new task.

The method asks the foundation model to compare pairs of observations and indicate which better matches the stated goal. It then learns a reward function from these preference labels. This choice addresses the noise and inconsistency that can arise when a model is prompted to assign raw reward scores directly.

Experiments demonstrate effective learned rewards and policies in classic control and in manipulation involving rigid, articulated, and deformable objects. Under the same assumptions, the method outperforms prior approaches that use large pretrained models for reward generation. The results support pairwise visual preferences as a useful source of reward supervision, with the text goal and visual observations supplying the task information needed by the approach.
icml-2024-rl-vlm-f-reinforcement-learnin.tldr: RL-VLM-F learns reward functions from a vision-language model's preferences between observations, using a text goal without human reward supervision.

paragraphs: Conditional stochastic optimization models decisions under uncertainty. Much of its existing theory assumes independent data, even though dependence appears in applications such as time series, operational control, and reinforcement learning. This paper studies sample average approximation for that dependent-data setting, asking whether its established statistical guarantees can be retained.

The analysis combines covariance inequalities with an independent-block sampling technique. Under conditions described as mild, the authors prove asymptotic consistency and a finite-sample guarantee. Consistency concerns the behavior as data accumulates, while the finite-sample result addresses accuracy with a limited amount of data; both extend the theoretical basis for using the approximation with dependence.

The paper also establishes sample complexity O(d/ε⁴), matching the order reported for independent-data cases. Experiments across several applications support the theory and show no performance degradation from dependence in the tested real-data settings. The implication is conditional: the analyzed dependence need not worsen the sample-complexity order, and the empirical results support practical use in the applications examined.
icml-2024-sample-average-approximation-f.tldr: Under mild conditions, sample average approximation retains consistency and independent-case sample-complexity order for conditional optimization with dependent data.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether poisoned training data can cause text-to-image diffusion models to reproduce copyrighted images under particular prompts. It formalizes a copyright-infringement attack and introduces SilentBadDiffusion, a backdoor method that does not require access to or control over the training process. The vulnerability studied lies in data incorporated into an otherwise clean dataset.

At a high level, the method disperses copyrighted information across poisoning data while connecting pieces of that information with text references. The authors describe this construction as inconspicuous when mixed with clean data. The central concern is that apparently unobtrusive training examples can establish a targeted behavior without changes to the fine-tuning pipeline.

Experiments show that models trained with a poisoning ratio of 0.20% can generate copyrighted images when given specific prompts. The results also indicate that more sophisticated diffusion models are easier to attack in the studied settings. These findings expose a potential weakness in copyright-protection strategies: stronger generative capability can coincide with greater susceptibility to this form of data poisoning.
icml-2024-the-stronger-the-diffusion-mod.tldr: SilentBadDiffusion demonstrates that subtle data poisoning can trigger copyrighted-image generation, with stronger diffusion models more susceptible in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: A reward model can rank language-model outputs the same way after a monotone transformation, yet the transformed scores can change how optimization behaves. This paper studies which transformation to use and how to combine rewards for multiple desired properties. It derives an answer through a probabilistic interpretation of alignment with Bradley–Terry preference models.

The proposed LSC transformation applies a log-sigmoid function to centered rewards. It emphasizes improving poorly performing outputs over increasing the scores of outputs that already perform well. The authors show how this mitigates underfitting, where some prompts receive little improvement, and reward hacking, where optimization exploits inaccuracies in the reward model.

The transformation also gives reward aggregation a logical interpretation: summing transformed rewards connects to the probability that an output is good on all measured properties, in the paper's precise formulation. Experiments using reinforcement learning from human feedback to improve helpfulness and harmlessness show substantial gains over untransformed rewards. The work therefore links reward scaling, optimization priorities, and multi-property alignment in one framework.
icml-2024-transforming-and-combining-rew.tldr: LSC transforms preference rewards to emphasize weak outputs and gives their combination a probabilistic interpretation for satisfying multiple properties.

paragraphs: TROVE helps language models solve tasks by writing programs with reusable high-level functions. Programs built entirely from primitive functions can become verbose and error-prone, while manually designing higher-level helpers requires expertise. The paper asks code models to build and maintain those helpers themselves, reducing the human work involved in creating a useful toolbox.

The method requires no training. It develops the toolbox while generating solutions, using existing functions, adding new ones, and periodically trimming the collection. This ties reusable function creation to the tasks being solved and keeps the resulting collection compact. The same pipeline produces different functions for mathematics, table questions, and image reasoning.

Across 11 datasets, TROVE produces simpler, more accurate solutions than the reported CodeLLaMa baselines and previous GPT-based methods, with toolboxes that are 79–98% smaller. Human verification is also reported to be 31% faster and 13% more accurate than with baselines. These findings connect compact reusable abstractions to both automated task performance and the ease of checking generated programs.
icml-2024-trove-inducing-verifiable-and-.tldr: TROVE builds and prunes reusable function toolboxes without training, yielding simpler, more accurate programs that people can verify more efficiently.
